# Architecture

VastX Native's goal is React Native/Flutter for the Nuxt ecosystem: Vue
components rendered as real native views, not a WebView. This document is
the honest map of what that requires, what's implemented, and what isn't —
so contributors know exactly where the frontier is.

## Why NativeScript, not a from-scratch renderer

A "true native renderer" needs two things a WebView-based tool (Capacitor,
Ionic) doesn't: a JS runtime with native marshalling (so JS can call
`UIView`/`android.view.View` APIs directly, no bridge-over-HTTP, no WebView
process), and a Vue renderer that creates native view instances instead of
DOM nodes. Building both from scratch is most of what NativeScript itself
is — a mature, years-old project. Reinventing it would be a multi-year
detour before a single native view ever appeared on screen. VastX Native
builds *on* NativeScript's runtime and on `nativescript-vue`'s renderer,
and focuses its own effort on the part that's actually missing: Nuxt's
developer experience layered on top of that renderer.

## Why not Nuxt's own build pipeline (Vite/Nitro)

Nuxt's builder assumes a browser target: it generates a client entry that
mounts Vue to a DOM node, and Nitro exists to produce a server response to
hydrate. Neither applies here — there's no DOM node, and `ssr: false` on
native builds means there's no server response either. Rather than fight
Nuxt's builder internals to make it emit something it wasn't designed to
emit, VastX Native uses Nuxt only for what it's actually good at in this
context — file-based page discovery, the module/auto-import system, config
— and hands the actual on-device bundle to NativeScript's own webpack-based
toolchain, which already knows how to produce a native bundle correctly.

```
app/pages/*.vue  ──(pages:extend hook)──►  route manifest  ──►  useNativeRouter()
                 ──(vastx-native CLI scan)──►  .vastx-native/app.js  ──►  ns run/build
```

Two independent consumers read the same page tree: the Nuxt module (via
`pages:extend`, for editor/type-checking DX and the manifest `vue-tsc` sees)
and the CLI (via a standalone filesystem scan, since `init`/`dev`/`build`
run outside Nuxt's dev server). See `src/build/generate-routes.ts` and
`cli/lib/scan-pages.mjs` — they implement the same file-based routing
conventions independently on purpose, rather than sharing a runtime
dependency between a Nuxt-hooked build step and a standalone CLI process.

It has no concept of `display`, `position`, `overflow`, or CSS grid at all (layout is chosen by container type — `StackLayout`/`FlexboxLayout`/`GridLayout`/`AbsoluteLayout` — never by a CSS property), and its `transform` value parser (`convertToTransform` in `style-properties.js`) expects literal numbers, not the `var(--tw-translate-x)`-style CSS custom properties Tailwind v3 composes its transform utilities from — so running Tailwind's full generated stylesheet as-is would silently no-op most of it. Fixed scope instead: `tailwind.config.cjs` ships with `corePlugins` as an *allowlist* (not the full utility set) of only the utilities that map to confirmed-supported properties (spacing, color, typography, borders/radius, opacity, shadow, visibility, z-index, and the flex-* properties scoped to `<FlexboxLayout>`) — pinned to Tailwind **v3** deliberately, since v4 dropped the JS-config `corePlugins` API this relies on. A new `<NFlex>` component (a bare, unstyled `<FlexboxLayout>` wrapper) is what flex utility classes (`flex-col`, `items-center`, `gap-4`, ...) actually apply to, the same way flex utilities only do anything on a real flex container on web — verified this is a real, working NativeScript CSS property (not just a name match) by reading `flexbox-layout-common.js`'s property registrations directly. `@nativescript/webpack` already runs every `.css` file through `postcss-loader` and merges in a project's own `postcss.config.js` (confirmed by reading `postcss-loader`'s own `getPostcssOptions` merge logic, not assumed from its config comment) — so wiring Tailwind in needed no changes to the webpack config generation at all, just a `postcss.config.cjs` exporting `require('tailwindcss')`, plus `generateEntry()` now copying a project's own `app/app.css` into `.vastx-native/app.css` (the exact relative path `app-css-loader` resolves, confirmed by reading its source) on every regenerate. **Verified end-to-end without a device**: ran the real `tailwindcss`+`postcss` pipeline against the actual generated `tailwind.config.cjs`/`postcss.config.cjs`/`app.css`/starter pages in a scratch project, then fed the expanded output through the exact same `css` parser package `css2json-loader` uses — confirmed 11 rules parsed cleanly with plain literal values (`padding: 1.25rem`, `background-color: #4f46e5`, `flex-direction: column`), not CSS variables, meaning NativeScript's property converters will actually apply them. **Scoped to Android for now, by design, not oversight**: `<FlexboxLayout>` on Android delegates straight to a native Java widget (`org.nativescript.widgets.FlexboxLayout`) — no concern there — but on iOS there's no native flexbox engine in UIKit, so NativeScript ports the actual flexbox algorithm to JS and runs it in `onMeasure`/`onLayout` (1,291 lines of JS-side layout math per `FlexboxLayout` instance, vs. `StackLayout`'s 157-line thin native pass on the same platform) — mature and shipped in core, but a real, unmeasured performance question for deeply nested trees specifically on iOS, which already carries the same "unverified" flag as the rest of this framework. Not yet run against a real device (same limitation as everything else needing an SDK/Xcode this sandbox doesn't have). **Two real gaps found from actual retrofits, now fixed**: this initially only merged to a feature branch, so installing the default `github:vastx-tech/vastx-native` spec got none of it — merged to `main`. And the three config files were only ever written by `create`'s one-time scaffold, so re-running `vastx-native init` on a project that predated this (the exact way `init` is supposed to bring a project up to date) silently did nothing — `ensureTailwindSetup()` (`cli/lib/tailwind-setup.mjs`) now writes all three from `init` too, only if missing, so it can't clobber a project's own customizations. That first fix then surfaced a second: `init` never installs `tailwindcss`/`postcss` themselves (only `create`'s generated `package.json` declares them, and only `create` runs `npm install`) — `postcss.config.cjs`'s `require('tailwindcss')` threw `Cannot find module 'tailwindcss'` on a real retrofit. Fixed by having `ensureTailwindSetup()` check resolvability (`createRequire(...).resolve()`) and `npm install --save-dev` both packages only when actually missing. Verified all three fixes for real: a scratch project with no Tailwind files gets all three generated; a customized `tailwind.config.cjs` survives a second run untouched; and a project missing `tailwindcss` gets it installed live (confirmed via a real `npm install`), with a second run correctly staying silent once it's resolvable. |
| `useWebSocket()` (`src/runtime/composables/useWebSocket.android.ts`/`.ios.ts`, `cli/lib/websocket-setup.mjs`) | **Android: fully verified on real hardware** — real Gradle build, real install, real device, real remote WebSocket server, open/receive/send/echo all confirmed live. iOS unverified like every other iOS path here. | NativeScript has no global `WebSocket` (confirmed on real hardware: `typeof WebSocket` is `"undefined"`) and no maintained NativeScript WebSocket plugin exists on npm (checked directly, nothing real found). `@nativescript/core`'s own HTTP module uses its own native widget (`org.nativescript.widgets.Async.Http.MakeRequest`, confirmed by reading its Android implementation directly), not OkHttp, so OkHttp isn't guaranteed on the classpath just from depending on core — `vastx-native init` now adds it as a real Gradle dependency via `App_Resources/Android/app.gradle` (the same real `apply from:` mechanism used for version management, reusing the same `ensureMarkedBlock()` helper — factored out of `app-version.mjs` once this became the second real caller needing "coexist with a project's own content and with another managed block in the same file" idempotency). The Java interop (`okhttp3.WebSocketListener.extend({...})` to subclass an abstract Java class from JS) is confirmed as NativeScript's real, standard convention by reading three independent usages directly in `@nativescript/core`'s own source (`ui/frame/activity.android.js`, `fragment.android.js`, `index.android.js`) before writing this, not invented. Since OkHttp itself has no npm type definitions (a Java library, not a JS one), a minimal ambient `okhttp3.d.ts` was added covering only the classes/methods actually used, keeping the rest of the project's typecheck fully clean rather than silently degrading it. <br><br>**A real, non-obvious bug caught before shipping**: this is the framework's first platform-split composable (`.android.ts`/`.ios.ts`, the same convention `@nativescript/core` itself uses) exposed through the package's `"./runtime/*"` wildcard export. Importing it with the same `.js` suffix every other composable uses (`useWebSocket.js`) fails — reproduced directly via a real webpack compile — because the package's exports-field wildcard resolves to an exact target file *before* webpack's own platform-extension list (`.android.js`/`.ios.js`/`.js`) ever gets a chance to run, and no bare `useWebSocket.js` exists, only the two platform variants. Dropping the suffix (`'vastx-native/runtime/composables/useWebSocket'`) lets webpack apply its extension resolution to the wildcard-substituted path correctly — confirmed both the failing and working form with real compiles, not assumed. Documented clearly in the composable's own doc comment and the README, since it's a real, easy-to-hit trap for the first person to add a second platform-split composable. <br><br>**Two more real bugs caught only by finishing the on-device verification, not by compiling**: (1) OkHttp 5.x split a `com.squareup.okhttp3:okhttp-android` artifact out of the main `okhttp` artifact, and that artifact's AAR metadata requires `compileSdk` 37+ — a real `checkDebugAarMetadata` Gradle failure against this project's (NativeScript's own default) `compileSdk` 35. Fixed by pinning to OkHttp **4.12.0** (the last pre-split 4.x major, no such requirement) in `cli/lib/websocket-setup.mjs`, rather than forcing every project to bump `compileSdk` just to satisfy one dependency. (2) Android blocks cleartext (`ws://`, non-TLS) traffic by default for apps targeting API 28+, so a real device immediately failed with "CLEARTEXT communication to 127.0.0.1 not permitted by network security policy" — the same class of problem Flutter/React Native solve with a debug-only network security config. Fixed the same way: `App_Resources/Android/src/debug/res/xml/network_security_config.xml` (cleartext permitted only for `127.0.0.1`/`10.0.2.2`/`localhost`, only in debug builds — release builds get no such exception) plus a matching `App_Resources/Android/src/debug/AndroidManifest.xml` overlay referencing it. Confirmed both fixes with real rebuilds, not assumed. <br><br>**The actual verification, end to end, on real hardware**: `@nativescript/types` was added as a real devDependency (neither Android nor iOS ambient globals — `okhttp3` aside — existed before this) and wired into `tsconfig.json`'s `types` field, confirmed clean by the exact "Cannot find name" errors it fixed. A real webpack compile of a 14-page app (the same real, full-sized app used for the MCP client's verification, plus one temporary test page) succeeded. A real `gradlew.bat assembleDebug` produced a real, installable APK. `adb install` put it on a real, physically connected Android device. A real Node.js WebSocket server (the `ws` package, port 8181) was bridged to the device over USB with `adb reverse tcp:8181 tcp:8181`. On launch: `[wstest] open` fired, then `[wstest] message: hello from real ws server` — the server's own greeting, received live. Tapping a real on-screen button (verified by screenshot, then `adb shell input tap` at the button's actual on-screen coordinates) sent `ping from device`; the server logged `received: ping from device` and echoed it back; the device logged `[wstest] message: echo: ping from device`. Every leg of open/receive/send/receive confirmed live, not assumed. iOS has the same "written against Apple's real documented API, never compiled" status as every other iOS path in this framework. |
| MCP client (`src/runtime/composables/useMcpClient.ts`) | Implemented, verified against a real MCP server; not yet confirmed on an actual device | The mobile-viable subset of MCP's "Streamable HTTP" transport — its non-streaming mode. Determined by real, on-device capability checks this session (not assumption): NativeScript's runtime has `fetch`/`XMLHttpRequest` but no global `WebSocket` and no `EventSource` (confirmed via a real diagnostic page logging `typeof` each, run on physical Android hardware), ruling out MCP's stdio transport (no subprocess spawning on mobile anyway), WebSocket transport, and streaming Streamable HTTP (server-initiated messages need `EventSource`-style SSE parsing). What's left — POST a JSON-RPC message, read an `application/json` response directly instead of a stream — is confirmed spec-compliant by reading the real `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` client transport's own source: it's exactly the code path that SDK itself falls back to against a non-streaming server, not a simplification invented here. <br><br>**Verified against a real server, not just reasoned about**: stood up a real `StreamableHTTPServerTransport` (`mcp-server/test-http-server.mjs`) and ran the exact request sequence this composable uses with plain `fetch` — `initialize` (captured the real `mcp-session-id` response header), `notifications/initialized`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, with the session id correctly echoed on every subsequent request. This also caught a real, non-obvious behavior difference: the transport's *stateless* mode (tried first) requires every request to be independently self-contained, which doesn't fit a client that initializes once and calls tools afterward — switched to *stateful* mode (also the realistic mode a real remote MCP server would run in), which worked correctly end to end. Also confirmed this file compiles cleanly through the real native webpack build, alongside a real, full-sized, unrelated app (13 real pages) with zero errors and zero changes needed to any of them. **Not yet confirmed**: running inside an actual compiled NativeScript app on a physical device against a network-reachable MCP server — needs real network topology (device and server on the same LAN) this session didn't have available to set up. |
| Pinia support (`isPiniaInstalled()`/`renderAppEntry()` in `cli/lib/generate-entry.mjs`) | Implemented, verified via a real webpack compile with the actual store code confirmed in the emitted bundle | Prompted directly by a user push-back: "install nuxt modules like pinia" doesn't work generically, because most Nuxt modules deliver their functionality through Nuxt's own Vite/Nitro build hooks — hooks the native build never runs at all, since it's a separate NativeScript webpack pipeline end to end (confirmed earlier: only `@nativescript/webpack`'s base config + `nativescript-vue`'s `chainWebpack` construct it). Pinia is the exception, not a special case: its actual store engine is just Vue reactivity with zero DOM dependency. Checked directly, not assumed — downloaded pinia@4.0.3 and `@vue/devtools-api@8.1.5` via `npm pack` and grepped their real dist output: zero references to `document`/`localStorage`/`navigator`/`window` anywhere except a single `IS_CLIENT = typeof window !== "undefined"` guard that every DOM/devtools code path (`registerPiniaDevtools`, the devtools plugin, a file-`saveAs` helper) is gated behind — and NativeScript's runtime never defines a global `window` (confirmed by grepping `@nativescript/core`), so `IS_CLIENT` is always `false` and none of those branches ever execute. `@vue/devtools-api`'s `setupDevtoolsPlugin` import is static (needs to resolve for webpack even though it's never called), so it's pulled in as a real dependency too. Everything Pinia imports from `vue` (`effectScope`, `getCurrentInstance`, `inject`, `markRaw`, `toRaw`, `toRefs`, ...) resolves through the existing `vue` → `nativescript-vue` alias, since `nativescript-vue` re-exports `* from '@vue/runtime-core'` directly (confirmed against its actual entry file), and its pinned `@vue/runtime-core` version comfortably satisfies Pinia's `vue: ^3.5.11` peer requirement. Wired in as opt-in, not forced: `generateEntry()` checks whether `pinia` is resolvable from the project (`createRequire(...).resolve('pinia')`) and only then emits `import { createPinia } from 'pinia'` + `.use(createPinia())` in the generated `.vastx-native/app.js` — confirmed both branches produce the expected bootstrap. **Verified end-to-end, not just at the config level**: a real scratch project with `pinia`/`@vue/devtools-api` actually installed, a real `defineStore`-based counter store, and a page calling it from `@tap` — compiled with a real `webpack()` invocation (`webpack 5.111.1 compiled successfully`, zero errors), and the emitted `vendor.js`/`bundle.js` were grepped directly to confirm Pinia's real core code and the store's own `useCounterStore`/`increment` logic are actually present in the output, not just that resolution succeeded. |
| HTML tag names (`src/runtime/html-elements.ts`, `src/runtime/vue-compat.ts`) | **Removed** — both files deleted, along with the `vue` webpack alias override and `registerHtmlElements()` call that wired them in | Removed in favor of steering usage toward the framework's own N*-prefixed native primitives instead of HTML-lookalike tags — the project's own `STYLING.md`/`AGENTS.md` already warn against a browser mental model (no `overflow`, no block formatting, single-child `ScrollView`) elsewhere, and this tag sugar was in tension with that: across the whole repo (framework, reference app, scaffold templates) actual usage amounted to a single `<div />` root wrapper, since replaced with `<StackLayout>`. The `vue-compat.ts` `vModelText` shim was tied specifically to `<input>`'s removal (`@vue/compiler-dom` special-cases `v-model` on the literal tag names `input`/`select`/`textarea` regardless of runtime registration) and had no independent reason to exist once that tag was gone, so it and its high-order `chainWebpack` alias override were removed together rather than left as dead code with a stale justification. Full original implementation history kept below for provenance. A direct follow-up to a user push-back on "can we compile HTML to NativeScript" — full arbitrary HTML/CSS fidelity is out of scope (that's browser-engine-scale work, not a framework feature; see the README's "HTML tag names" section for the case made against attempting it). What's real and buildable: `nativescript-vue` exposes a public `registerElement(name, resolver, meta)` API — the exact mechanism it uses internally for `<StackLayout>`/`<Label>`/etc (confirmed by reading its element registry directly) — so `div`/`p`/`img`/`input`/`h1`–`h6`/`a`/`strong`/`b`/`em`/`i` and several purely-semantic containers (`ul`/`ol`/`li`/`header`/`footer`/`nav`/`main`/`section`/`article`/`aside`/`form`) now register as real native views this same way. `button`/`label`/`span` needed no registration at all: tag matching is case/hyphen-insensitive (`normalizeElementName`), and nativescript-vue's own `Button`/`Label`/`Span` registrations already collide with those lowercase HTML names. Confirmed this isn't short-circuited by Vue's compiler treating real HTML tag names as literal DOM elements (a real risk unique to these tags, unlike custom names like "StackLayout"): nativescript-vue never uses `@vue/runtime-dom` at all, and its own `NSVElement` constructor calls the same registry's `getViewClass(tagName)` for *every* element vnode regardless of which compiled form produced it — verified by reading `NSVElement`'s constructor and `nodeOps.createElement()` directly. <br><br>One real, compiler-level difference *did* surface, and it took real debugging to pin down: `@vue/compiler-dom` compiles `v-model` on tags it recognizes as native HTML form elements (`input`/`select`/`textarea`) to `withDirectives(vnode, [[vModelText, value]])`, importing `vModelText` from `'vue'` — but `nativescript-vue` has no such export (it re-exports `@vue/runtime-core`, not `@vue/runtime-dom`). Reproduced directly: a real compile of `<input v-model="x">` warned `export 'vModelText' was not found in 'vue'`. Fixed with a new `vue-compat.ts` (re-exports everything `nativescript-vue` does, plus a real `vModelText` modeled on `@vue/runtime-dom`'s own implementation but reading/writing `NSVElement`'s `text` property and listening for the real `textChange` event instead of DOM `input`/`change`), aliased in as `'vue'` in the generated `webpack.config.cjs`. Getting the alias to actually win took a second, genuinely non-obvious round of debugging: a same-order `chainWebpack` override looked correct and even proved itself correct via direct instrumentation (`config.resolve.alias.get('vue')` immediately reflected the override) — but the *final* resolved config still had the old value. Root cause, found by reading `@nativescript/webpack`'s `resolveConfig()`/`applyExternalConfigs()` directly rather than assumed: it scans every dependency for its own top-level `nativescript.webpack.js` and auto-registers it, meaning `nativescript-vue`'s alias-setting chain function gets registered *twice* — once by this project's own explicit `require('nativescript-vue/nativescript.webpack')(webpack)` call, and again by that auto-discovery, which runs *inside* `resolveConfig()` itself, strictly after anything the config factory registers directly, regardless of registration order. A same-order override can never win against that; only an explicit higher `chainWebpack(fn, { order: 10 })` does, confirmed by instrumenting the exact chain before and after applying the fix. <br><br>**Fully verified with a real webpack compile**, not just resolved config: a scratch project with a page using every new tag (`div`/`h1`/`h3`/`p`/`strong`/`em`/`img`/`input v-model`/`a`/`ul`/`li`/`button`) compiled with `webpack 5.111.1 compiled successfully` — zero errors, zero warnings (the `vModelText` warning included) — and the emitted `vendor.js`/`bundle.js` were grepped directly to confirm real `registerElement("div", ...)` calls, the `HtmlParagraph`/`HtmlAnchor`/etc. classes, and `vModelText`/`getModelAssigner` are genuinely present in the compiled output, not just that resolution succeeded. Not yet run on an actual device (same limitation as everything else needing an SDK/Xcode this sandbox doesn't have). |
| Gradle memory tuning (`ensureGradleMemorySettings()` in `cli/lib/gradle-tuning.mjs`) | Implemented, verified with a real clean rebuild | Directly reported: "the Gradle building process... taking too much memory." Traced to `@nativescript/android`'s own scaffolded `platforms/android/gradle.properties`: `org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx16384M`, a flat 16 GB Gradle daemon heap ceiling baked into the template regardless of the machine actually running the build. Confirmed against the reporting user's real machine: `Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem`/`Win32_OperatingSystem` showed 5.74 GB of *total* physical RAM — a heap ceiling nearly 3x the entire machine's memory. This plausibly explains more than just slowness: the same session hit repeated, unexplained `'gradlew.bat' is not recognized` spawn failures from the CLI's own child-process invocation (confirmed via `android-plugin-build-service.js`/`gradle-command-service.js`'s source that both just do `spawnFromEvent('gradlew.bat', ...)` relying on `cwd`) despite the file demonstrably existing and running fine when invoked directly — severe memory pressure is a known cause of intermittent Windows `CreateProcess` failures, though this wasn't isolated as the sole cause. <br><br>Confirmed this file has no built-in App_Resources override the way `app.gradle` does (no reference to `gradle.properties` anywhere in the `nativescript` CLI's own source — it's scaffolded once by `@nativescript/android`'s own template copy during `platform add`, never regenerated on subsequent `prepare`/`build` calls), so a one-time patch immediately after `platform add` is durable. `ensureGradleMemorySettings()` computes a replacement `-Xmx` from the machine's actual total RAM (originally 35%, clamped to 768 MB–3 GB; lowered to 25% / 768 MB–2 GB after the 3 GB ceiling still crashed an external developer's 8 GB Windows machine), adds `kotlin.daemon.jvmargs` (Kotlin's compiler runs its own separate JVM, also worth capping) and `org.gradle.workers.max=2`, and marks the file with a comment so reruns never clobber a value a project has since customized. Verified the computed values are sane across a realistic range (2 GB machine → 768 MB floor; 5.74 GB → 2057 MB; 16 GB+ → 3072 MB ceiling, confirmed by direct calculation, not just eyeballed), confirmed idempotency (byte-identical file on a second run), and — the real test — reran `gradlew.bat --stop` then a full clean `assembleDebug` on the actual affected project with the new ~2 GB ceiling: identical successful build (57 tasks executed, 42 up-to-date) with a fraction of the memory. |

Worked around at the call-site level instead: reference the name once in `<script>` (a `computed()`, or a plain function for a per-item value in a `v-for`) rather than calling it inline in the template — which is also better Vue practice regardless (cached vs. re-run on every render). |

| Auto-import loader — comment/semicolon-free-code false positive (`cli/lib/auto-import-loader.cjs`) | Fixed, verified with a real on-device crash reproduced and resolved | Another bug this session's own auto-import feature (added earlier the same day) had, caught only by finishing real on-device testing of the reference app: the "already imported" check used `[^;]*` to bound its regex scan to "within one statement" — which only works for semicolon-terminated code. This framework's own generated/example code is semicolon-free, so with no semicolon to bound the scan, `[^;]*` could match from the first `import` keyword all the way to *any later* `from` anywhere in the file — including through doc comments that happen to mention the target name (exactly what happened: a comment in `ProductCard.vue` explaining *why* `formatCurrency()` was moved into `<script>` for auto-import's own sake ironically contained the words "import"/"formatCurrency"/"from" in a pattern that made the loader falsely believe the name was already imported, and silently skip injecting it). Neither "compiled successfully" nor a clean typecheck caught this — only inspecting the actual compiled bundle content and then a real device launch did. Fixed by bounding the scan to a single line (`[^\n]*`, multiline flag) instead of "until the next semicolon", which both handles semicolon-free style correctly and narrows any remaining comment-collision risk to the same line only. Verified past the regex fix itself: the compiled bundle now shows a correctly bound `__webpack_require__` call in place of the bare reference, and the app launches and renders correctly on the real device that previously crashed. |

A native `<Button>` uses `setOnClickListener` instead. Reproduced on the device: 5 quick double taps (100 ms apart) on the old `NButton` counted 5 of 10. On Android `NButton` now attaches a native `View.OnClickListener` on `loaded` (iOS keeps `@tap`; UIKit's single-tap recognizer fires every tap) and sets a `RippleDrawable` foreground masked to its corner radius. After: filled and outline `NButton` both counted 10 of 10, matching a native `<Button>`; a disabled `NButton` counted 0 of 10; the ripple was visible mid-press. Any other `@tap` on a plain view still has this limitation, now listed in STYLING.md's Android pitfalls. |
| `v-tap` directive for any view (`src/runtime/native-tap.ts`) | **Verified on a real Android 16 device** | Follow-up to the `<NButton>` row above, for views that aren't buttons (cards, rows, steppers). `attachNativeClick()` holds the Android `View.OnClickListener` + masked `RippleDrawable` logic (ripple radius from the view's own `borderTopLeftRadius`) and re-applies it on every `loaded`; `<NButton>` now uses it too. `vTap` wraps it as a directive (`el.nativeView` is the NativeScript view in nativescript-vue's directive hooks; the handler is read from per-element state so `updated` can swap it), falling back to the plain `tap` event on iOS. Registered by the generated entry (`.directive('tap', vTap)`) and declared in `GlobalDirectives` (a non-function value is a vue-tsc error). On the device, 5 quick double taps from a count of 1: a `v-tap` card went to 11 (10/10), an `@tap` card to 6 (5/10), as expected. One earlier batch read 19 and 20 for the two cards; single slow taps counted exactly 1 each and the rerun was exact, so that batch is attributed to input injected while the app was still starting, but it wasn't reproduced. |

| `ProductCard`'s nested tap gesture conflict (`examples/reference-app/app/components/ProductCard.vue`) | Fixed, verified on a real device with a precise, isolated repro | A real, on-device-only UX bug: the original component put `@tap` on the outer `NCard` (navigate to product detail) with an `NButton` ("Add to cart") nested inside it. NativeScript's tap gesture recognizers don't stop propagation to an ancestor's own, separately-registered listener the way DOM `stopPropagation()` does — confirmed directly by isolating the repro (tap the button, track Pinia cart count across a controlled navigate-back-and-check sequence): a single tap on "Add to cart" fired *both* handlers, silently adding the item **and** navigating away, every time. Fixed by making the tappable name/description/price area and the `NButton` siblings instead of ancestor/descendant — no shared `@tap`-bearing ancestor, no conflict. Worth calling out as a load-bearing lesson for this framework's own docs, not just this one component: nesting any tappable element inside another tappable element's hit area needs this same sibling restructuring, since there's no gesture-level fix available. |

Every property's exact valid values came from grepping every `cssName:` registration across `@nativescript/core/ui/` directly and reading each one's own `valueConverter`/enum, not from documentation — this caught a real bug in an earlier draft of `flex()`, which allowed `justify: 'space-evenly'` even though NativeScript's flexbox implementation (`flexbox-layout-common.js`) only supports the CSS Flexbox Level 1 subset (`flex-start`/`flex-end`/`center`/`space-between`/`space-around`) — confirmed directly, not assumed from CSS spec familiarity. `1rem = 16dip` is an explicit, documented convention borrowed from CSS (NativeScript has no root-font-size concept of its own), not a native feature. `opacity()`/`shade()`/`tint()` (Flutter's `Color.withOpacity()`/`shade*`) do real hex/rgb math; confirmed `rgba(...)` strings are genuinely parsed by NativeScript's own `Color` class (`color-utils.js`), not just hex, before relying on that format. | iOS Info.plist missing required keys (`cli/lib/ios-infoplist-fix.mjs`) | Fixed, verified with three independent real-device findings, a real download-and-diff against NativeScript's own template, and a regression test suite | The very first real bugs iOS verification surfaced: `ns platform add ios` scaffolded `App_Resources/iOS/Info.plist` with only `CFBundleDisplayName`/`CFBundleName` — missing everything else a real, working iOS app needs. Confirmed the exact gap by downloading and extracting the real `@nativescript/template-hello-world-ts@9.1.1` package and diffing its own shipped `Info.plist` against the broken one reproduced fresh on a `vastx-native create --platforms ios` project — every key this fix adds is present in the real template and missing from the broken one. Three distinct, independently-confirmed findings trace back to this: (1) `CFBundleExecutable` missing → `xcrun simctl install` fails with `"missing or invalid CFBundleExecutable in its Info.plist"` (also documented in NativeScript's own tracker, `github.com/NativeScript/nativescript-cli#4048`); (2) no launch-screen key at all → the app installs and launches but doesn't fill the screen — iOS falls back to legacy scaled compatibility mode without one, confirmed on a real physical device (initially misdiagnosed by this session as a `ScrollView` safe-area double-count — see the row above; that fix may still be independently correct, but wasn't the cause of the missing-content symptom); (3) a real, live project's broken scaffold can *also* be missing the `LaunchScreen.storyboard` file itself, not just the `Info.plist` key pointing at it — caught by a second real-device session that had already applied an early version of this fix and found `UILaunchStoryboardName` pointing at a file that genuinely doesn't exist anywhere in that project (`App_Resources`, `platforms/ios`, nowhere — confirmed by that session directly on the affected project, not assumed). None of these three are vastx-native-authored bugs (neither of this framework's own two `Info.plist`-touching code paths caused it — `app-version.mjs` only runs on an explicit `vastx-native version` command, and `splash.mjs` never touches `Info.plist`, only image assets, even though it does write into `LaunchScreen`'s own `Assets.xcassets` imagesets successfully — a separate, unaffected file from the storyboard itself). Fixed the same way this framework handles every other scaffolding gap: `ensureIosInfoPlistKeys()` inserts `CFBundleDevelopmentRegion`/`CFBundleExecutable`/`CFBundleIdentifier`/`CFBundleInfoDictionaryVersion`/`CFBundlePackageType`/`CFBundleShortVersionString`/`CFBundleSignature`/`CFBundleVersion`/`LSRequiresIPhoneOS`/`UIRequiresFullScreen`/`UIRequiredDeviceCapabilities`/`UISupportedInterfaceOrientations` (+ `~ipad`)/`UIApplicationSceneManifest` if entirely missing (values as raw plist XML fragments, so boolean/array/dict-valued keys work the same way as string ones), never touching a key that already has a value. The launch-screen key specifically checks whether `App_Resources/iOS/LaunchScreen.storyboard` actually exists on disk first: if it does, writes `UILaunchStoryboardName` pointing at it; if not, falls back to `UILaunchScreen` as an empty dict — Apple's own real, documented storyboard-less launch-screen mechanism, which depends on no file at all. | iOS `useSafeArea()` insets stuck at zero on first render (`src/runtime/composables/useSafeArea.ts`) | **Confirmed fixed** — five rounds to the real root cause, one apparent regression that turned out to be a stale/failed deploy rather than a real reproduction, then a discriminating on-device test (tap-triggered background flash, decoupled from the counter's own state) passed on every tap | The third real iOS-only bug this session's device testing surfaced, and it explains why the "Decrement does nothing" report kept reproducing after the screen-fit and launch-screen fixes above: a real-device session isolated it by **swapping the two counter buttons' physical order** in the page and having the user retest — the failure moved with screen *position* (whichever button ended up bottom-most failed, regardless of whether it was Increment or Decrement), which ruled out any operator/compiler/ref-semantics theory (already independently disproven earlier by compiling `count++`/`count--` through the real Vue SFC compiler) and the separate, still-unconfirmed HMR/Frame-navigation lead in one test. Root cause, confirmed by reading `@nativescript/core`'s own source directly: on iOS, `Page.getSafeAreaInsets()` reads `nativeViewProtected.safeAreaInsets` (`ui/core/view/index.ios.js`) — a real UIKit property UIKit only populates after the view controller's own first native layout pass. `useSafeArea()`'s `measure()` ran once inside Vue's `onMounted()`, which fires when the native view is attached — a point that can race ahead of that first UIKit layout pass, leaving `insets.value` locked at `{0,0,0,0}`. `NPage`'s `contentStyle` applies that as `paddingBottom`, so on a device with no physical home button (a home-indicator device), the bottom-most element ends up flush against the screen edge, inside iOS's own system gesture strip — which can swallow single taps landing on it. The only thing that ever re-triggered `measure()` was `Application.orientationChangedEvent`, which ordinary single-orientation testing never fires, so it never self-corrected. Fixed by additionally re-measuring on the page's own `layoutChangedEvent` (confirmed real and genuinely cross-platform in `view-common.js`, fired from `_setNativeViewFrame` on both platforms — including deliberately on the very first layout even when the frame doesn't change, per that method's own comment, which is exactly the event this needed) — capturing the `page` reference once in `onMounted` and cleaning up both listeners from that same reference in `onUnmounted`, rather than re-querying `Frame.topmost()` at teardown time when the frame may have already moved on. Verified: root-caused and the fix validated by the real-device session directly; independently re-verified here by reading `_setNativeViewFrame` (both `index.ios.js` and `index.android.js`) to confirm `layoutChangedEvent` really does fire post-layout on both platforms, and by a clean `vue-tsc`/`eslint` pass. **Confirmed on the physical device once**, with a real control for the obvious confound: the same session temporarily rendered the live insets on-screen as a debug label next to the two buttons and specifically checked whether the extra label itself was just pushing content up rather than the fix genuinely working — insets read non-zero, Decrement responded correctly, and the debug label was removed afterward. **But the bug then reproduced again on a fresh rebuild**, pointing at a real remaining gap rather than a fluke: `layoutChangedEvent` only fires when a view's *frame* changes, and reading `viewSafeAreaInsetsDidChange`'s own real implementation (`ui/page/index.ios.js`) shows it's a genuinely *separate* UIKit callback from the one that sets a view's frame — so the page's own outer frame can easily stay identical across an insets update, meaning `layoutChangedEvent`'s one guaranteed first-layout fire is not a reliable enough signal that insets are actually populated by the time it lands. Hardened with a short, bounded retry (`MAX_MEASURE_ATTEMPTS = 5`, ~32ms apart) that keeps re-measuring only while the reading is still all-zero, alongside the existing listeners — confirmed with a standalone algorithmic smoke test, but this **also reproduced the bug again**, specifically on a fresh `--clean` rebuild rather than a warm relaunch. Root-caused a third time by reading `viewSafeAreaInsetsDidChange` fully: it no-ops entirely (`if (this.isRunningLayout || !this.didFirstLayout) return`) if insets change before the page's first layout completes — very plausible on a cold process start, whose launch-transition latency is real and variable, unlike a warm relaunch; 160ms total wasn't a wide enough window for that case specifically. Fixed by adding `Page`'s own `navigatedToEvent` (confirmed real, `ui/page/page-common.js` — notified once the page's navigation transition genuinely completes, a materially later and stronger guarantee than any layout-pass event) as a third trigger, and widening the retry window substantially (`MAX_MEASURE_ATTEMPTS = 15`, 100ms apart — up to 1.5s total) to give a slow cold start real room, while a device that resolves immediately still exits on its first check. `layoutChangedEvent`/`orientationChangedEvent` both stay wired too — every round has only ever added a signal, never removed one that might still matter in some case not yet observed. That third round **also reproduced** — but this time as a **flat, permanent zero** for the entire 1.5s retry window, on a device (iPhone XS) independently confirmed to genuinely have non-zero insets, not intermittently as the first two rounds' theories would predict. That result doesn't fit a pure timing race at all: a real race should self-correct *somewhere* in 1.5s; a value that never once changes points at the underlying reference being wrong from the start, not just read too early. Root cause, found on a fourth pass by reading `frame-common.js`'s `setCurrent()` directly: `Frame.currentPage` only flips (and `Page.navigatedToEvent` only fires) once `_processNextNavigationEntry()` actually processes the queued navigation entry — asynchronous relative to `nativescript-vue`'s own `Frame` `nodeOps.insert()` call (`frame.navigate({ create: () => child.nativeView })`, the same mechanism implicated in the still-open HMR/back-button bug below) that triggers it. If this composable's `onMounted` — inside the very page being navigated to — ran before that queue drained, `Frame.topmost()?.currentPage` could read `null` or the *previous* page, captured once into a closure variable and never corrected: every listener and the retry loop kept reading that same wrong reference forever, exactly matching a flat, unrecoverable zero regardless of retry-window length. The fourth round's fix was to stop depending on `Frame.topmost()` at all: `useSafeArea()` accepted an optional `Ref` to the exact `Page`, and `NPage.vue` passed a template ref on its own `<Page>` element (`ViewBase.page`, `ui/core/view-base/index.js` — a plain getter walking `this.parent.page` up a view's real parent chain, confirmed real — would have been the same category of fix; the explicit ref was used instead since `NPage.vue` already owns the exact `<Page>` in question). **This crashed the app on launch on every page**, confirmed via `xcrun devicectl device process launch --console`: a native `tns::NativeScriptException`, signal 6 (SIGABRT) — independently reproduced by the real-device session with a minimal, unmodified counter page, ruling out any test scaffolding as the cause. A real regression, not a partial fix, and reverted immediately. One structural detail was flagged as possibly relevant (the compiled render function emitted `ref: "pageRef"` with no accompanying `ref_key`) but investigated and reasoned to likely be a red herring: independently recompiling `NPage.vue`'s real source through the actual `@vue/compiler-sfc` pipeline confirmed `ref_key` genuinely is absent, but also confirmed `bindingMetadata` correctly identifies `pageRef` as `'setup-ref'` — `ref_key` omission is expected, standard behavior for *non-inline* template compilation (what this project's webpack/`vue-loader` setup uses throughout, not a defect specific to this one ref), and `nativescript-vue`'s renderer's unmodified `@vue/runtime-core` component instance handling (`proxyRefs`) should resolve a plain string ref against `$setup` correctly regardless. The actual crash cause was not confirmed (no on-device JS stack trace was obtainable — `devicectl` couldn't route console output, no Xcode-attached symbolicated crash report was available). Rather than keep guessing at an unconfirmed native crash with no way to reproduce it locally, the ref-based approach was abandoned entirely: `NPage.vue`'s `<Page>` reverted to a plain, ref-free tag, and `useSafeArea()` reverted to `Frame.topmost()`-based resolution — but fixed for the actual confirmed race (round 4's root cause remains correct) by **never caching the page at all**: `measure()` now re-resolves `Frame.topmost()?.currentPage` fresh on every call, including every retry tick, so once `Frame`'s navigation queue actually drains — well within the 1.5s window already confirmed sufficient in round 3 — it naturally starts reading the real, current page instead of a permanently-stale one. Event listeners self-heal the same way: `measure()` (re-)attaches them to whichever page it just resolved, migrating off a previous one if a different page shows up later. Verified with a clean `vue-tsc`/`eslint` pass, a real webpack compile of the reference app confirming the emitted bundle no longer contains any `pageRef`/ref-on-`<Page>` reference at all, and a standalone algorithmic smoke test covering the queue-drains-after-a-few-ticks case, the listener-migration case, and the resolves-immediately case. **Confirmed working across two separate `--clean` rebuilds plus one warm rebuild** — no crash, both counter buttons responded correctly every time on each of those three runs. A subsequent *fourth* rebuild (warm, only difference being an unrelated debug `Label` removed) reproduced the original tap-unresponsive symptom again with no crash — so the fix looked real but not yet fully deterministic; see the separate device-pixel/DIP unit bug below, found in the same file while investigating this. **That apparent non-determinism turned out to be a false alarm**: the "fourth rebuild failed" report was against a deploy that had actually failed silently (a device-connection blip the wrapper script didn't surface as a non-zero exit), not a real reproduction. Once genuinely redeployed (confirmed via grepping the deployed bundle for the DIP fix's own `toDeviceIndependentPixels` call, and an explicit "Successfully synced" in the deploy log before retesting), a discriminating test was run specifically to separate "the tap gesture isn't reaching JS" from "it reaches JS but doesn't update": Decrement's handler was temporarily changed to flash the page background alongside the normal count logic. Every single tap flashed the background *and* updated the count, with no misses — real, direct evidence the gesture recognizer was never the problem, and this fix is genuinely correct. One residual, unconfirmed detail noted but not investigated further: the user described it as taking "some time" to settle after a fresh launch before feeling fully responsive — plausibly just the retry window itself (rounds 3–5 already established this can take up to ~1.5s on a cold start) rather than a new bug, but not root-caused. |
| iOS `getSafeAreaInsets()` unit mismatch — device pixels stored as DIPs (`src/runtime/composables/useSafeArea.ts`) | Fixed, confirmed by reading the real conversion function and matching its output against a real device's actual measurement | Found while confirming the round-5 fix above on a real device: the on-screen debug insets read `top=264 bottom=102 left=0` on an iPhone XS — a real bottom safe-area on that device is 34pt, and 102 ÷ 3 (that device's real screen scale) = 34 exactly. Root cause, confirmed directly in `ui/core/view/index.ios.js`: `getSafeAreaInsets()` runs UIKit's real `safeAreaInsets` (in points) through `layout.toDevicePixels()` before returning it — i.e. it deliberately returns device pixels, not DIPs — but `NPage`'s `contentStyle` hands that number straight to a NativeScript padding style property, which expects plain DIPs like every other numeric style value in this framework. The result was ~3x too much edge padding reserved on that 3x-scale device (proportionally worse on any higher-density screen), which likely wasn't blocking anything on its own — if anything, the extra padding probably made the "does not fill the screen" era of this bug harder to trigger, not easier — but is a real, independent bug. Fixed by converting back with the real, confirmed inverse (`Utils.layout.toDeviceIndependentPixels()`, `utils/layout-helper/index.ios.js` — `value / getMainScreenScale()`, the exact inverse of `toDevicePixels`'s `value * getMainScreenScale()`) before storing into `insets.value`. Android is unaffected either way: it has no override of `getSafeAreaInsets()` at all, so it always returns the base class's hardcoded `{0,0,0,0}` (a separate, pre-existing, out-of-scope limitation — Android's own safe-area handling isn't wired through this API), and dividing zero by a scale factor is still zero. Verified with a clean `vue-tsc`/`eslint` pass and a real webpack compile. |
| `gap`/`row-gap`/`column-gap` silently drops a `<FlexboxLayout>`'s (`<NFlex>`'s) last child entirely on Android (`cli/lib/native-tailwind.cjs`, `cli/lib/scaffold-templates.mjs`, `src/runtime/style.ts`) | **Confirmed fixed on a real Android device** | The actual cause of a real user report — a fresh `vastx-native init android` project's scaffolded counter template rendered with its Decrement button missing entirely and "the height got cut." Initially misdiagnosed as the Android safe-area/edge-to-edge row above (a real, independently-worthwhile fix, but not what caused this) before a real device screenshot and a `uiautomator` view-hierarchy dump showed the Decrement button wasn't clipped or off-screen — it simply didn't exist as a native child at all, only 4 of the template's 5 flex children were present in the tree. Root-caused with a live HMR session against the real device: swapping the two buttons' order moved the failure with them (whichever button was *last* disappeared, cold-restart or HMR, regardless of which button or its `variant`), and removing `gap-4` fixed it immediately; a follow-up isolated test set only a raw inline `row-gap: 16` (no Tailwind, no column-gap) and reproduced the exact same last-child drop, conclusively isolating the cause to NativeScript's own compiled `org.nativescript.widgets.FlexboxLayout` Android widget itself — a real upstream bug, not something introduced by this framework's Tailwind adapter or how it splits `gap` into `row-gap`/`column-gap`. Not fixable from JS (the widget is a compiled native library, no source available to patch), so fixed by removing `gap` support outright rather than leaving a utility that can eat content: dropped `'gap'` from `TAILWIND_CORE_PLUGINS` (Tailwind no longer generates `gap-*` classes at all) and removed `gap`/`row-gap`/`column-gap` from `native-tailwind.cjs`'s property-preservation exception list (any raw `gap` a user writes directly in CSS now gets stripped by `@nativescript/tailwind`'s own upstream filter, same as any other property it doesn't recognize, rather than passed through to the broken native setter). The typed style helper's `flex({ gap, rowGap, columnGap })` still exists (a separate code path, not Tailwind) but now carries an explicit warning in both its type and this doc, since it sets the exact same native property and would hit the identical bug. The scaffolded counter template and every `gap-*` usage in the reference app and docs were converted to per-child margin utilities (`mb-4` in a column, `mr-2`/`mr-4` in a row, on every child but the last) — the standard safe substitute, and now this framework's own documented convention (`STYLING.md`). Verified: a 6→8-assertion update to the existing `cli/tests/styling.test.mjs` suite (confirms `gap-*` classes are no longer generated at all, and that raw `gap` in custom CSS is now stripped rather than preserved), a clean `vue-tsc`/`eslint` pass, and — the real confirmation — rebuilding `dist/` and redeploying to the actual affected Android device via a live HMR session: both buttons appeared, and repeated taps on each independently changed the counter value correctly. |
| Kebab-case template attributes on native elements silently no-op app-wide (`src/runtime/components/*.vue`, `eslint.config.mjs`) | **Confirmed fixed on a real Android device**, found and root-caused by a peer session working on a real client app | Reported by a peer session as `<NPage>`'s ActionBar never actually hiding despite no `title` prop and no `actionBar` slot anywhere in a real ~28-page app — every condition in `NPage.vue`'s own `:action-bar-hidden="!title && !$slots.actionBar"` binding was already correctly `true`, ruling out the app's own code. Root-caused by that session tracing `nativescript-vue`'s actual patch pipeline directly (`dist/renderer/patchProp.js` → `dist/dom/index.js`): a template attribute name is passed **completely literally** into the npm `set-value` package against the native view (`setValue(this.nativeView, name, value)`), with no hyphenate/camelize step anywhere in that path — confirmed independently here by reading the same two files. `:action-bar-hidden="true"` therefore executes `nativeView['action-bar-hidden'] = true`, a nonsense property nothing reads, instead of `nativeView.actionBarHidden = true`, the real property Android's rendering code checks — the binding silently no-ops, `actionBarHidden` stays at its default (`undefined`/falsy), and Android shows a default ActionBar with the app's own label as title. Confirmed on-device by that session via `adb shell uiautomator dump`: a real native ActionBar (~48dp, text "heritagebyaemli") present with zero `<NPage>` in the app passing a `title`. This is **not** a `<Page>`/`actionBarHidden`-specific bug — it's a property of `nativescript-vue`'s renderer itself, affecting *any* kebab-case template attribute bound onto a **native** element (`<Page>`, `<ScrollView>`, `<Label>`, `<Switch>`, `<TextField>`, `<Image>`, `<StackLayout>`, ...) anywhere in this framework's own components — critically, it does *not* affect this framework's own `<N*>` SFC components (`<NPage title="...">` etc.), since Vue's real component-prop resolution (`defineProps`) already handles kebab-to-camel matching correctly there; the bug is specific to the *native element* rendering path only. A systematic sweep of every `.vue` file in `src/runtime/components/` (prompted directly by that session's own suggestion to check for the same pattern elsewhere) found it was far from isolated: `NText`/`NBadge`/`NButton`'s `:text-wrap`/`text-wrap` (Label never actually wrapped/not-wrapped as intended), `NButton`/`NSwitch`'s `:is-enabled` (**`disabled`/`loading` never actually disabled the native tap/switch, only the visual styling** — a real, meaningful interaction bug, not cosmetic), `NSwitch`'s `:off-background-color`, `NInput`'s `:max-length`, `NBottomSheet`'s `vertical-alignment`, and — the highest-impact ones — `NetworkImage`/`CachedImage`'s `load-mode`/`use-cache`/`:decode-width`/`:decode-height`, meaning the `decodeWidth`/`decodeHeight` performance optimization these two components' own comments specifically call out ("a 4000px source shown at 120dip would otherwise fully decode into memory at its native size on every load") **had never actually been applied since either component was written** — every remote/cached image in every app built on this framework has been decoding at full source resolution regardless, and `NetworkImage`'s documented `useCache: false` default (deliberately opposite of `Image`'s own `useCache: true` Android default, "always re-fetches") was silently reverting to `true` (always cached) instead. Fixed every instance found by converting the attribute name to camelCase (never changing the bound value/logic itself) — no exceptions found where kebab-case coincidentally worked. Additionally added an explicit `hideActionBar?: boolean` prop to `NPage` (an independent suggestion from the same peer session): when omitted, visibility is still inferred from title/slot presence exactly as before; when passed, it's an unambiguous override, useful for any app (like the one that found this) building a fully custom in-content header. Hardened against this exact bug class recurring: `eslint.config.mjs` now flips `vue/attribute-hyphenation` to `'never'` (require camelCase) for every `.vue` file in this repo — the rule's own default (prefer kebab-case, a real convention for actual DOM/HTML templates) is exactly backwards here and would have auto-"fixed" every one of these bugfixes back into the bug. Verified: a clean `vue-tsc`/`eslint` pass (confirming the new lint rule itself doesn't flag any of the fixes, and would flag a reintroduction), and the original `NPage` ActionBar fix independently confirmed fixed on-device by the reporting session via a before/after `uiautomator` dump. The broader sweep's other fixes (`NButton`/`NSwitch` disabled state, `NetworkImage`/`CachedImage` decode sizing/caching) are corrected at the same source-verified level as the original finding but have not each individually been re-confirmed on a real device one by one. |
| Android `useSafeArea()` insets permanently zero, hiding content under the system nav bar (`src/runtime/composables/useSafeArea.ts`) | Fixed via real source/API confirmation, not yet device-confirmed | Reported directly by a user: a fresh `vastx-native init android` project's scaffolded counter template rendered with its Decrement button not visible and "the height got cut" — on Android, not iOS. Root cause, confirmed by reading `@nativescript/core` directly (the same gap already noted, but left unaddressed, in the DIP-mismatch row above): `getSafeAreaInsets()` has no Android override anywhere in the package — only `ui/core/view/index.ios.js` overrides it — so the base `view-common.js` implementation (`return { left: 0, top: 0, right: 0, bottom: 0 }`) is genuinely all Android ever returns, unconditionally. That alone would just mean "no padding," not "content hidden" — the second half of the cause is that `application.android.js` calls the native `enableEdgeToEdge(activity)` helper unconditionally on *every* activity, on every Android version this runtime supports (confirmed reading the call site directly, `onActivityCreated`, no config flag gating it) — so page content always draws full-bleed under the status bar and the gesture/3-button navigation bar. With insets permanently zero, `NPage`'s `contentStyle` never compensates, so the bottom-most element (the scaffolded template's Decrement button) ends up rendered underneath the system navigation bar instead of above it. Fixed by giving `useSafeArea()` a real Android-specific measurement path: `Device.os === 'Android'` branches to a new `getAndroidSystemBarInsets()`, which queries the page's own native view directly via Java interop — `View#getRootWindowInsets()` (real platform API, `@since 23`, confirmed present in `@nativescript/types-android`'s ambient declarations), then `WindowInsets#getInsets(WindowInsets.Type.systemBars())` (`@since 30`) on current devices, falling back to the older `getSystemWindowInset{Top,Bottom,Left,Right}()` accessors (deprecated in API 30 but still functional) on API 23–29, and leaving insets at their existing value on anything older than API 23 rather than risking a call to a method that doesn't exist at that API level. Every method/class/field name used (`getRootWindowInsets`, `WindowInsets.Type.systemBars`, `android.graphics.Insets`' `top`/`bottom`/`left`/`right` fields) was confirmed directly against the installed `@nativescript/types-android` `.d.ts` before writing this, the same discipline the original iOS pass used. The raw values these APIs return are device pixels exactly like iOS's `safeAreaInsets`, so the same confirmed inverse (`Utils.layout.toDeviceIndependentPixels()`) converts them back to DIPs — verified this divides by the real Android display density (`getDisplayMetrics().density`, `utils/layout-helper/index.android.js`), not a hardcoded or iOS-specific scale factor. The existing retry/listener machinery (`measureWithRetry`, `layoutChangedEvent`, `navigatedToEvent`) needed no changes — it already re-invokes `measure()` repeatedly regardless of platform, which covers the same "native view not attached to a window yet" race on Android that `getRootWindowInsets()` can hit (returns `null` before the first layout, handled by returning `undefined` and letting the retry loop continue). Verified: a clean `vue-tsc --noEmit` pass (confirming every Android interop type signature actually resolves against the real ambient types, not just plausible-looking guesses) and a clean lint pass. **Not yet confirmed on a real Android device** — no Android hardware/emulator was reachable from this session when this fix was written; needs the same kind of on-device confirmation (rendering the live inset values, or just visually confirming the Decrement button now sits above the nav bar) every other platform-specific fix in this table got before being called done. |
| iOS `NPage` scrollable safe-area double-counting (`src/runtime/components/NPage.vue`) | **Hypothesis fix, not yet device-confirmed** | Second real iOS symptom this framework's verification surfaced: on a real device, `NPage`'s default `scrollable` page cut content off before the bottom of the screen (a button below several other elements was entirely missing/off-screen), a class of bug only ever possible on iOS — Android has shown no such symptom despite the *exact same* `contentStyle` padding logic being exercised there already. Root-caused by reading `@nativescript/core`'s own `ui/scroll-view/index.ios.js` directly: `ScrollView`'s `iosContentInsetAdjustmentBehavior` defaults to `'never'` (not Apple's own recommended `'automatic'`), which makes its `onLayout()` subtract `getSafeAreaInsets()` from its *own* internal `contentSize` math — the source even comments on this exact risk class ("doing both makes contentSize track the dynamic navbar height and causes scroll drift"). `NPage`'s `contentStyle` *also* applies `useSafeArea()`'s insets as manual `padding` on the content inside that same `ScrollView` — meaning, on iOS specifically, the safe area was plausibly being accounted for twice: once by ScrollView's own internal geometry, once by this component's own padding. Fixed by setting `ios-content-inset-adjustment-behavior="automatic"` on the `ScrollView` (a no-op on Android — this property's `affectsLayout` is Apple-only in the source), handing iOS's own portion of inset handling to native `UIScrollView` behavior instead of NativeScript's internal geometry subtraction, leaving this component's own manual padding as the only place it's now applied. **Explicitly not yet confirmed on a real device, and likely NOT the actual cause of the reported missing-content symptom** — a separate real-device investigation (see the `UILaunchStoryboardName` row below) found the actual cause of that specific symptom to be a missing launch-screen reference, a much more classic and precise match for "app doesn't fill the screen" than a scroll-inset double-count would be. This `ScrollView` change is still a real, source-grounded correctness fix in its own right (the double-counting risk it addresses is real, per `@nativescript/core`'s own comment), and is left in — just no longer treated as the explanation for the bug that prompted it. |
| VS Code extension (`vscode-extension/`) | Implemented at MVP scope, unverified inside an actual VS Code window | Commands for every `vastx-native` CLI command, a device picker (`ns device --json`), and hot-restart/force-restart/toggle-watcher/stop controls. The controls run everything inside a real `vscode.window.createTerminal()`, not a headless spawned process — confirmed by reading NativeScript's own `key-command-helper.js` that `ns run`'s interactive key commands (`r`/`R`/`w`/Ctrl+C) require a real TTY (`stdin.setRawMode`) and silently fall back to an unwired IPC listener otherwise, which a plain `child_process.spawn` with piped stdio would hit. `ns device --json`'s exact output shape was confirmed by reading `ListDevicesCommand`'s source, not guessed. Verified as far as possible without a running VS Code instance: compiles cleanly against the real `@types/vscode` API (`npx tsc`), and packages successfully with `@vscode/vsce` into a structurally valid `.vsix` (`@vscode/vsce@4` itself has an ESM/`parse5` interop bug on this Node version — pinned to `@vscode/vsce@^3.9.2`, which doesn't). **Not verified**: has never actually been loaded into a VS Code extension host and clicked through — that requires a running VS Code instance this environment doesn't have. |
| Typed style helper expansion (`src/runtime/style.ts`) | Implemented, verified with lint/typecheck and an isolated real-execution smoke test | Rounded out the property set against the same `cssName:` grep-and-read-the-`valueConverter` discipline the original pass used: `tintColor()` (a genuine inherited `Style` property, `tintColorProperty.register(Style)` in `image-common.js` despite living in that file — not Image-only), `placeholder()` (`placeholder-color`, `editable-text-base-common.js`), `flex()`'s `wrapBefore` (`FlexWrapBefore.parse` confirms a real boolean flex-item property), and `textStyle()`'s `stroke`/`variationSettings` (`text-stroke`'s real shorthand format confirmed via `css-stroke.js`; `font-variation-settings` left as a raw string — its own source has no clean enum, just axis/value pairs). `resolveLength`/`resolveColor` were exported (previously module-private) so components needing a real DIP/hex value for imperative APIs (see `NSkeleton` below) don't reimplement them. |
| `NContainer`/`NetworkImage`/`CachedImage`/`NSkeleton` (`src/runtime/components/`) | Implemented, verified with lint/typecheck (no device run yet — same sandbox SDK limitation as other UI-kit additions) | Four new UI-kit components, alongside removing the HTML compat layer (see that row above) so `NFlex`/`NContainer` stay the two genuinely-different layout primitives (multi-child flex vs. single-child decorated box) rather than one being renamed into the other's job. `NContainer` wraps `ContentView` (confirmed already registered by nativescript-vue itself, `nativescript-vue/dist/nativescript/elements.js`) with the existing `box()`/`padding()`/`margin()`/`size()`/`align()` helpers as props. `NetworkImage`/`CachedImage` wrap `<Image src="...">` (which already loads remote URLs natively) with a loading spinner and a `#fallback` slot; since `ImageBase` fires only one real event (`isLoadingChangeEvent`, confirmed by grepping every `Event = ` / `notify(` call in `ui/image/*.js`), failure is detected the only way the source allows: the property-change event's own `object` (confirmed real shape `{ object, value, oldValue }` from `properties/index.js`) still has no `imageSource` once loading finishes. `useCache` (the two components' real point of difference) is confirmed Android-only by direct comparison of `index.android.js` (sets it, passes it into the native `ImageView.setUri` call) against `index.ios.js` (no trace of it at all) — documented as an honest asymmetry rather than a fabricated cross-platform cache. `NSkeleton`'s shimmer is `View.animate({ translate, iterations: Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY, curve: 'linear' })` — genuine, confirmed infinite-loop support (both `index.android.js` and `index.ios.js` special-case `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` directly) — sweeping a `linear-gradient` band clipped to the placeholder's own bounds via `clip-path: inset(0)` (the only real clipping primitive NativeScript has), stopped on unmount via the animation promise's own confirmed-real `.cancel()`. |
| Performance: image decode sizing + list recycling (`NetworkImage`/`CachedImage`, `examples/reference-app/app/pages/index.vue`) | Implemented, verified with a real webpack compile | Two concrete FPS levers, not just README advice: `decodeWidth`/`decodeHeight` (real `ImageBase` properties, read by both platforms' `_createImageSourceFromSrc` before the bitmap is even allocated) are now set on `NetworkImage`/`CachedImage` to the same resolved DIP number as `width`/`height`, capping decode resolution to what's actually displayed instead of the source's full resolution. The reference app's product list was converted from a plain `v-for` (every item a permanent live view) to a real, view-recycling `<ListView>` (`recycleNativeView: 'auto'`) — which required `NPage :scrollable="false"` on that page, since a `<ListView>` needs to be the *one* bounded-height scrolling container: nesting it inside `NPage`'s default `<ScrollView>` would force it to measure its full unbounded content height to fit the outer scroller, defeating recycling entirely (the same "nested scrollables" trap this project's own `STYLING.md` already warns about for `ScrollView`). The list gets the header/button's leftover space via `flexGrow: 1` in the page's flex column — the same real flex-item property `flex()`'s own `grow` option sets. Verified with a real `webpack()` compile of the reference app (clean, zero errors/warnings) exercising both changes together. |
| MCP server (`mcp-server/`) | Implemented, verified end to end with a real MCP client against a real device | Exposes `doctor`/`build`/`lint`/`clean`/`analyze`/`version`/`list_devices`/`install_and_launch`/`read_logs` as MCP tools, each calling the exact same `cli/commands/*.mjs` functions the real CLI uses — no separate implementation to drift out of sync. The one real technical risk: this server talks over **stdio**, meaning stdout *is* the JSON-RPC protocol channel, but `doctor()`/`build()`/etc. `console.log` directly and spawn child processes (`ns info`, `ns build`) that inherit real stdio — either would corrupt the connection. Fixed at the shared layer: `cli/lib/run.mjs` now exports `withCapturedOutput()`, an ambient module-level toggle that makes `run()` pipe+buffer instead of inherit, and captures `console.log`/`console.error`, restored even if the wrapped function throws — with zero changes needed to any of the five existing command files, and zero behavior change for the real CLI's own direct terminal usage (toggle defaults off). Verified directly: ran `doctor()` through it for real and confirmed zero output reached the surrounding process's actual stdout, with the full 13-check report correctly captured instead. **Verified end-to-end, not just at the unit level**: used the MCP SDK's own real `Client` + `StdioClientTransport` (not a mock) to spawn the real server and drive it over the real protocol — `listTools()` returned all 8 tools; `doctor` returned the complete captured report; `list_devices` correctly surfaced a real, pre-existing, legitimate error (`ios-device-lib` `ENOENT` — no iOS tooling on this Windows machine, not a bug here); and with a real connected Android device, `install_and_launch` performed a real `adb install`+`am start` and `read_logs` returned real, current `logcat` output confirming the app actually launched. |
| HMR live-reload pushes a duplicate page with a back button (`nativescript-vue`, not this framework's own code) | **Root-caused, not yet fixed** | Surfaced on iOS during the safe-area investigation above: editing a page's own `<script>`/`<template>` and letting LiveSync reload it while sitting on that page (no prior navigation) shows an ActionBar with a back button plus a duplicated title, as if a second copy of the page got pushed onto the Frame's navigation stack instead of the root being cleanly replaced. Root cause, confirmed by reading `nativescript-vue`'s own source directly (`nativescript-vue/dist/nativescript/elements.js`, `registerElement('Frame', ...)`): a `<Frame>`'s `nodeOps.insert` calls `frame.navigate({ create: () => child.nativeView })` whenever a `<Page>`-type child is inserted, but `nodeOps.remove` is a **documented no-op** — its own comment says "a Page removed by Vue stays on the native backstack; navigation out of a Frame is only driven through `$navigateBack`/`$navigateTo`" (it even logs a real `__DEV__`-gated warning to this effect: `"Removing the current <Page> from a <Frame> has no effect on the native navigation stack."`). Vue's own generic reconciliation model (unmount the old vnode, mount the new one) is exactly what a page-level HMR reload does when the changed component is a *child* of `<Frame>` rather than the true app root — `nativescript-vue`'s own root-reload HMR handling (`keepPlaceOnRootReload` in the same package) only special-cases a reload of the literal root component, not an arbitrary `Frame`-child page reload, so this case falls through to ordinary Vue reconciliation and hits the no-op `remove`/real `navigate` asymmetry. This is a real gap in `nativescript-vue` itself, not something this framework's own code causes or can fully paper over from the outside. **Workaround**: fully restart the app (stop `ns run`, force-quit, relaunch) after a page-level edit instead of trusting LiveSync's in-place reload, whenever a page other than the true root is being edited. Not yet fixed — a real fix would need either a `nativescript-vue`-level change (special-casing `Frame`-child HMR reloads the way the root already is) or a framework-level workaround (e.g. detecting HMR reload of a page component and calling `$navigateBack()` before the reload's own remove/insert cycle runs). |

## Roadmap

**Done**, moved out of "future work": a real Android device run completed
successfully (build, install, launch, render) after fixing everything that
run surfaced (`webpack.config.cjs`, `typescript`/`tsconfig.json`,
`"type": "module"`, `main`/`bundlerConfigPath`/`webpackConfigPath`) — see
the status table above for the full trail; the UI kit now covers
buttons/text/input/card/switch/spinner/avatar/badge/divider/bottom-sheet
/modal/container/network-image/cached-image/skeleton, past the original
`<NPage>`/`<NActionBar>`/`<NTabs>` set; and iOS has now also run end to
end on a real physical device (install, launch, full-screen rendering,
safe-area layout, tap/gesture responsiveness), with four real bugs found
and fixed along the way — see the status table's iOS-specific rows.

1. Wire `unplugin-auto-import`/`unplugin-vue-components` into the
   NativeScript webpack build the CLI hands off to, so composables/
   components auto-import identically in editor DX and on-device (right
   now native pages need explicit imports — see the "Auto-imports reaching
   the on-device bundle" row above).
2. iOS device verification so far covers `NPage`/safe-area layout and the
   counter app's own tap handling — not every code path yet. Specifically
   still unverified on a real iOS device: `useWebSocket()`'s iOS half
   (`NSURLSessionWebSocketTask`), Tailwind/`<NFlex>` rendering (landed
   Android-scoped on purpose — see its own status-table row), and the rest
   of the UI kit beyond what's exercised by the reference app's counter/
   product pages.
3. Further UI kit components (list, action sheet)
   and a real device confirmation for the
   ones just added (`<NButton>` etc. are verified via webpack compile only
   so far, same caveat every fresh addition here starts with).
4. Port more of Nuxt's file-based routing conventions (route groups,
   layouts-equivalent) into `generate-routes.ts`/`scan-pages.mjs`.
5. The VS Code extension (`vscode-extension/`) now exists at MVP scope —
   see its status-table row. It has never been loaded into an actual VS
   Code window; that's the next real test for it, the same way a real
   Android device was the real test for everything else here. Also not
   yet done: publishing it to the Marketplace (needs a publisher account
   this repo doesn't have set up), and packaging/publishing it isn't
   wired into any release process yet.
6. CI: a real device-farm or simulator smoke test for both platforms, now
   that both have had at least one manual real-device run.
7. Tailwind/`<NFlex>` support landed Android-scoped on purpose (see its
   status-table row) — now that iOS has real device access, the two real
   follow-ups: an actual on-device (not just pipeline-level) confirmation
   that Tailwind utility classes render correctly, and a real nested-
   `FlexboxLayout` layout-cost benchmark on iOS hardware (using
   NativeScript's own `Trace.categories.Layout` plus Xcode Instruments'
   Time Profiler) before deciding whether `<NFlex>` is safe as iOS's
   default primitive too, or needs a lighter-weight iOS-specific fallback.
8. The still-open HMR/Frame-navigation bug — see its own status-table row
   above for the full root cause. Has a known workaround (a full app
   restart instead of relying on LiveSync) but no real fix yet.
8. `<NGrid>` (a real `<GridLayout>` wrapper) doesn't exist yet — Tailwind's
   `grid-cols-*` utilities can't map to it the way flex utilities map to
   `<NFlex>`, since NativeScript's grid is configured via `columns`/`rows`
   template-string properties, not a CSS property at all. Needs its own
   translation layer, not just an allowlist tweak.
9. iOS needs the same real-device confirmation Android has. Releases are
   tagged on GitHub (`github:vastx-tech/vastx-native#vX.Y.Z`); `vastx-native`
   isn't on npm yet (the old `nuxt-native` package is, up to v2.2.1). Each
   release commits a prebuilt `dist/`, so installing an app never compiles
   the framework.
10. `useWebSocket()`'s iOS implementation needs the same on-device
    confirmation every other iOS path here still needs (Android is now
    fully verified on real hardware).
